title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
hook: Labs rarely disclose their data mixture recipes — but WARP shows you can recover a fine-tuned model's training-domain proportions just from its released weights, no training data required.
key_points: Training data mixtures (how much of each domain a model was fed) are rarely disclosed, leaving researchers unable to see the distribution that produced a released model.
Prior methods like membership inference only detect individual samples, not the corpus's overall composition.

WARP interpolates between a base and fine-tuned model via model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a 'geometric footprint' of the training data in weight space.
Geometric features from those footprints map to domain proportions via a simple softmax readout or a trained MLP.
On BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with mean absolute error as low as 0.046 and 0.104 — beating membership inference and even a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
content_html: Foundation models get released to the public all the time; the data recipes behind them almost never do. Domain mixture weights — how much of each data source a model actually saw — stay hidden, leaving researchers able to study a model's behavior but not the distribution that produced it. WARP asks whether the weights alone give that away.
extra_html:
Reading a footprint out of merged weights

Prior tools like membership inference only tell you whether one sample was in the training set, not the corpus's overall shape. WARP instead interpolates between a model's base and fine-tuned checkpoints using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory. That approximated path exposes a geometric footprint of the training data in weight space, from which WARP extracts features and maps them to domain proportions — either with a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP trained on synthetic mixtures.

Why it matters

In controlled experiments on BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with mean absolute error as low as 0.046 and 0.104, respectively — outperforming membership inference and, notably, even a variant of itself given access to the true training trajectory. That's a meaningful result for model transparency and provenance: it suggests released weights leak more about how a model was built than labs might assume, with implications for auditing undisclosed training recipes.

related.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
related.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

flashcards.prompt: What access asymmetry does WARP address?
flashcards.back_html: Labs release model weights but rarely disclose the training data mixture that produced them, so researchers can study the model but not see the distribution it was actually trained on.

flashcards.prompt: How does WARP recover a training data mixture without access to the original training data?

choices.text: It interpolates between base and fine-tuned weights via model merging to approximate the missing trajectory, then reads a geometric footprint off that path
It performs membership inference on every individual training sample
It requires the lab to voluntarily disclose the mixture weights first

flashcards.explanation_html: Model merging generates pseudo-checkpoints that stand in for the actual training trajectory, and geometric features of that path are mapped to domain proportions.

flashcards.prompt: Why couldn't membership inference alone reveal a model's training data mixture?
flashcards.back_html: Membership inference detects whether individual samples were in the training set, but that's a per-sample signal — it doesn't characterize the overall domain composition of the corpus.
